title: Claude Code Plugins, Marketplaces & Nested Subagents
content:
## Overview

Through 2026, Claude Code's extension model matured from individual, manually-wired pieces (a hook here, an MCP server there) into a packaged distribution system: **plugins**, distributed through **marketplaces**, with a deeper **nested subagent** hierarchy underneath. This page covers the current architecture and the security risk that distribution model introduces.

---

## Plugins

A plugin bundles everything needed to add a capability to Claude Code into one installable unit: skills, hooks, subagents, and MCP server configuration. Plugin-provided skills are namespaced (e.g. `/my-plugin:review`) so that multiple plugins can coexist without colliding on command names. This mirrors how the layered architecture separates memory, hooks, skills, subagents, plugins, and MCP into distinct layers rather than one flat extension surface.

## Marketplaces

Plugins are distributed via **marketplaces** — a marketplace is just a metadata file (commonly hosted in a GitHub repo, but also distributable via npm or a team-internal registry) that lists available plugins and where to fetch them. Creating one requires no approval process: a single metadata file is enough to publish. Community registries like `claudemarketplaces.com` scrape GitHub roughly every hour to index newly published marketplaces automatically.

## Nested Subagents

Claude Code's subagent system now supports **hierarchical spawning**: a parent agent can create child agents, which can themselves spawn further children, by default up to three levels deep. This enables layered task decomposition for work that spans multiple modules or files — a coordinator delegates to module-level agents, which delegate further to file-level agents — without the coordinator having to manage every leaf task directly. Combined with per-agent cost attribution (tracking token spend per subagent in a fleet) and scoped permissions (restricting what each subagent tier is allowed to touch), this is the backbone of the "Workflow"-style orchestration used for large audits and migrations.

---

## The Marketplace Security Risk

The ease of publishing a marketplace is also its weakness. Security researchers at PromptArmor demonstrated an attack where a malicious plugin's Markdown instructions contain a hidden prompt injection: the plugin tells Claude it needs to "gather debugging context" and run a `curl` command to send that context to what looks like a debugging or RAG endpoint. Because the plugin frames the request as routine tooling rather than a risky action, it can bypass the human-in-the-loop approval prompt that would normally gate an unfamiliar network call — and the codebase data gets exfiltrated to the attacker's server instead.

A related class of attack, documented by SentinelOne and Prompt Security researchers, shows marketplace-distributed skills influencing which package registries or dependency versions get pulled into a project — a supply-chain angle on the same trust problem: once a plugin is installed, its instructions carry the same implicit trust as the user's own prompts.

Because automatic indexing (like `claudemarketplaces.com`'s hourly GitHub scrape) surfaces new marketplaces within about an hour of publication, a malicious marketplace can reach visibility almost as fast as a legitimate one. There is no vetting gate between "published on GitHub" and "discoverable in a marketplace directory."

**Practical mitigation:** treat installing a plugin from an unfamiliar marketplace the same as running an unreviewed shell script — read the plugin's hooks and skill definitions before installing, prefer marketplaces maintained by known organizations, and keep an eye on which permissions a plugin's hooks request.

---

## Why This Matters for This Playground

This repository's own wiki maintenance agent (`wikis/AGENT_PROMPT.md`) is itself a scheduled Claude Code prompt with git push access — the same class of automation that plugins package up for reuse. The marketplace risk above is a useful reminder that any automated agent with write/network access is only as trustworthy as the instructions it's given, whether those instructions come from a scheduled prompt, a hook, or a downloaded plugin.
